text: In 1882, a man was found dead under this oak tree in Arizona. Revolver in his hand. Boots gone. His feet wrapped in strips of his own shirt. His gun belt on upside down. And part of his scalp cut away. The jury called it suicide. His name was Johnny Ringo, one of the most feared gunmen in the Old West, and almost nobody believes the jury got it right. Wyatt Earp? Doc Holliday? A gambler with a grudge? He's still buried right where he was found. Which theory do you believe?

In 1886, the Army loaded nearly every Chiricahua Apache onto trains as prisoners of war, even the scouts who had served the Army. Somewhere in Missouri, as one train slowed on a steep grade, a man named Massai jumped. He was alone, in country he had never seen. Traveling only at night, he walked hundreds of miles back to the mountains of Arizona. He lived there in hiding for years and raised a family. Today, the highest viewpoint in America's newest national park carries his name. Massai Point.

America just got its sixty-fourth national park, and most people have never heard of it. Twenty-seven million years ago, a volcano here erupted with more than a thousand times the force of Mount St. Helens. The ash welded into rock, and ice carved it into thousands of stone pillars. Some boulders weigh hundreds of tons and balance on bases thinner than they are. Look at the horizon: the mountains form a giant face, staring at the sky. And a wild jaguar has walked these canyons. This is Chiricahua.
